construction.access_recipe: Page the resource with an explicit column list and a deterministic order: GET https://data.seattle.gov/resource/76t5-zqzr.json?$select=permitnum,permitclass,permitclassmapped,permittypedesc,description,housingunits,housingunitsadded,housingunitsremoved,estprojectcost,applieddate,issueddate,expiresdate,completeddate,statuscurrent,originalzip,relatedmup,totaldaysplanreview,numberreviewcycles,daysoutcorrections,dependentbuilding,standardplan,parentpermitnum&$where=permittypemapped='Building' AND issueddate>='2016-01-01' AND issueddate<='2022-09-30' AND estprojectcost>=50000&$order=permitnum&$limit=50000&$offset=0, incrementing $offset by 50,000 and stopping on a short page (24,750 rows means a single page suffices). Parse with json.loads or pandas.read_json(orient='records'); all timestamps are midnight floating timestamps so cast to date without timezone handling. Then: (1) drop rows with completeddate < issueddate or issueddate < applieddate, logging counts; (2) label y = 1 when completeddate is non-null and completeddate <= issueddate + relativedelta(months=48); (3) record the portal's stated last-updated date and rowsUpdatedAt from https://data.seattle.gov/api/views/76t5-zqzr.json as the pinned version; (4) never select or use statuscurrent, completeddate-after-window, latitude/longitude, contractor or applicant fields. The .csv form of the same resource path is interchangeable if the JSON parser is inconvenient.
construction.expected_size: Snapshot: 194,311 rows x 41 columns (portal metadata, 2026-11-14). Eligible release: 24,750 permits (3,841+3,779+3,669+3,981+3,154+3,460+2,866). Selecting ~22 columns gives an estimated 5-10 MB of JSON or CSV; a full 41-column pull of the entire dataset is roughly 200 MB (estimated, not measured here).
construction.format: Socrata SODA tabular resource over HTTPS (JSON records by default, CSV on the same path); one row per permit, 41 columns in the unfiltered snapshot
construction.source_examples: Documented value checks from the portal's own field statistics and live queries: PermitTypeMapped counts Building 155,941 / ECA and Shoreline Exemption 18,937 / Demolition 16,192 / Roof 2,133 / Grading 1,108 of 194,311; StatusCurrent counts Completed 135,018 / Expired 13,892; PermitClass counts Single Family/Duplex 113,167 / Commercial 43,400 / Multifamily 21,912 / N/A 6,946 / Institutional 5,769 / Industrial 2,643 / Vacant Land 474; IssuedDate non-null 141,321 and CompletedDate non-null 108,201 of 194,311. Second sample (6352649-CN): Multifamily / New / 807103.0000 / applied 2013-12-26 / issued 2016-01-07 / completed 2018-09-04.

evidence.claim: Dataset scope: a live snapshot of permits issued or in progress, 194K rows and 41 columns, refreshed daily and last updated 2026-11-14; it is a current snapshot, not an archive of historical vintages
evidence.quote: All building permits issued or in progress within the city of Seattle.

evidence.claim: The label event is administrative final-inspection completion, not occupancy or certificate of occupancy
evidence.quote: The date the permit had all its inspections completed.

evidence.claim: A missing CompletedDate is documented as still-under-inspection, which is why null is folded into y = 0 rather than dropped
evidence.quote: If there is an Issue Date but not a Completed Date, this generally means the permit is still under inspection.

evidence.claim: Portal licence designation and attribution metadata for this specific dataset
City open-data policy Section 1.D is the reuse basis: datasets are published with no registration, no licence requirement and no restrictions on use, which covers redistribution and modification
evidence.quote: Datasets on the Open Data Portal shall be made available without registration requirement, license requirement or restrictions on their use

evidence.claim: No mandatory credit line; attribution is preserved as a courtesy and as the dataset's own attribution field rather than as a licence condition
evidence.quote: Unless otherwise indicated, data on this site does not require specific attribution.

evidence.claim: Restriction that shapes field selection: data that is or can be configured as a list of individuals may not be used commercially, so contractor names, applicant-linked fields and street addresses are dropped and only ZIP is retained
evidence.quote: To the extent the data consists of a list of individuals or can be readily sorted, filtered, or configured as a list of individuals, it is not to be used for a commercial purpose.

evidence.claim: Non-completion is a substantial class, not a rare event: 5,565 of 7,325 Building permits issued in 2017 and 5,208 of 6,919 in 2019 carry any CompletedDate as of 2026-11
Eligible population observed directly: 3,841 / 3,779 / 3,669 / 3,981 / 3,154 / 3,460 / 2,866 for 2016..2022-09, summing to 24,750 permits

Row-level check of the eligible slice, including two quirks the construction code must handle: ExpiresDate is mechanically issued date plus 18 months (so it is not a useful feature) and CompletedDate can equal IssuedDate on the same day

limitations: The outcome is an administrative record: a physically finished project whose final inspection was never logged, or whose permit lapsed, counts as non-completion, so the label measures closure of the permit as much as completion of the work.

Current-vintage retrospectivity: EstProjectCost and HousingUnits are documented as subject to change if the project is modified, and the plan-review day columns are frequently null in 2016-era rows. Nothing here proves those fields were visible to an analyst in 2016; only that they are recorded on the current snapshot and are logically prior to issuance.

The dataset is a live, daily-refreshed endpoint with no immutable archive; a rebuild cannot reproduce the byte-identical extract. Labels for eligible cohorts are nonetheless stable because every 48-month window closed before 2026-09-30, so later refreshes can only add completions that fall outside the window.

The snapshot is a rolling window. Pre-2004 rows are sparse and 2004-2015 coverage is uneven, which is why the cohort window starts in 2016; older issuance dates in the file (including 1900-01-01 sentinels) must be filtered, not trusted.

The City's Terms of Use bar commercial use of data that is or can be configured as a list of individuals. Contractor names, applicant-linked fields and street addresses are therefore dropped and only ZIP is kept; this is a preservation obligation on the release, not a formality.

Single city and a single permitting authority, so external validity is limited to Seattle's permit regime; holdout cohorts for 2021-2022 also sit in a different construction-cost and post-pandemic regime than the training years, which is part of the task rather than an artefact to remove.

EstProjectCost >= 50000 is used both for eligibility and as a feature, so the population definition partly depends on a mutable declared field; a small number of projects revised upward after issuance can enter the cohort retroactively.

Deliberate exclusion of cross-row history means contractor track record, site-level phasing and prior-permit outcomes - the strongest real-world predictors - are absent; permits sharing a Development Site or ParentPermitNum remain correlated, so rows are not strictly independent across sibling permits of one project.
ExpiresDate is mechanically IssuedDate plus 18 months in the sampled rows, so permit duration carries almost no signal and is not used as a feature.

A same-day CompletedDate (issued and completed on the same date) occurs in the eligible slice, which suggests some permits are closed administratively on issue; such rows are kept because the documented field rule is unambiguous, but they depress the informativeness of the positive class.
reason: Seattle SDCI 'Building Permits' is a single no-account Socrata resource with 41 documented columns and an explicit portal designation of 'Public Domain' backed by a City of Seattle open-data policy that grants publication 'without registration requirement, license requirement or restrictions on their use'. Its CompletedDate field supplies a genuine forward outcome (final-inspection sign-off) that does not exist at issuance, and observed per-year counts give 24,750 eligible permits for 2016-01-01..2022-09-30 with a 16-24% positive rate, enough for fixed chronological train/eval/holdout splits within one modest worker's budget.

task.population: Every row in the live Socrata snapshot with PermitTypeMapped equal to Building, IssuedDate in the half-open window 2016-01-01 through 2022-10-01, and EstProjectCost at least 50000 nominal USD. Rows with impossible chronology (CompletedDate before IssuedDate, or IssuedDate before AppliedDate when both are present) are excluded as a source data-quality rule per the construction recipe. The unit is the permit as issued; no site-level or contractor-level aggregates are used. The population is fixed by permit type, issuance date and declared cost, not by the label value.
task.prediction_time: The permit IssuedDate, when the permit is issued. Only fields written at submittal, during plan review, or at issuance are used; CompletedDate, StatusCurrent, ExpiresDate and post-issuance revisions are excluded from features. The label is observed retrospectively after the 48-month window.
task.question: Will a newly issued Seattle building permit for a substantive construction project reach final inspection sign-off within four years of issuance?
task.simple_references: Majority-class control predicting completed for every row is 76-84 percent accurate depending on cohort. Calendar control uses issuance month only. Identity and structure control uses permit class, permit type and ZIP only. Persistence does not apply: each row is a single issuance event with no prior state inside the row, and prior-permit history is deliberately excluded; the nearest analogue is the class-group base rate already covered by the identity control.
task.split_policy: Fixed calendar boundaries on IssuedDate, no shuffling: train = 2016-01-01..2018-12-31 (11,289 eligible permits), eval = 2019-01-01..2020-12-31 (7,135), holdout = 2021-01-01..2022-09-30 (6,326). The holdout end date is chosen so the last 48-month label window closes on 2026-09-30, before the 2026-11-14 snapshot. No embargo is applied or needed: every feature is strictly row-local, there are no lags, rolling aggregates or other permits' outcomes, so moving a boundary by a month cannot leak anything.
task.target: y = 1 if CompletedDate is non-null and CompletedDate <= IssuedDate + 48 calendar months (dateutil relativedelta, month arithmetic); y = 0 otherwise, including permits still under inspection, expired permits and withdrawn permits. Evaluated against the 2026-11-14 snapshot, by which date the 48-month window of every eligible cohort has already closed, so the label can no longer flip from 0 to 1.
task.usefulness: The label is a four-year forward final-inspection sign-off that does not exist at issuance. Completion is the majority class (about 76-84 percent depending on cohort; non-completion about 16-24 percent), so the task is to separate the substantial stalling minority from projects that close out. It speaks to construction-pipeline attrition and permit-expiry workload. Because rows are single permits and no prior-permit history is used, the task is retrospective and row-local.

title: Four-year final-inspection sign-off of newly issued Seattle building permits
